en: Worship Govinda, worship Govinda,
worship Govinda, O fool.
When the appointed time has come and is near,
'ḍukṛñ karaṇe' will not, will not save you. (1)
Fool, give up the thirst for gaining wealth;
make your understanding good, and your mind free of thirst.
Whatever wealth you gain, earned by your own work,
with that content your mind. (2)
Seeing the weight of a woman's breasts and the region of her navel,
do not fall into the grip of delusion.
This is only a change of flesh, fat and the like:
think on it in your mind again and again. (3)
Water lying on a lotus leaf is very unsteady;
life is like it, exceedingly fickle.
Know that the world is seized by sickness and conceit,
and that all of it is struck down by grief. (4)
As long as you are bent on earning wealth,
so long is your own family fond of you.
Afterwards, when you live on in a worn-out body,
no one at home asks so much as a word of you. (5)
As long as the breath dwells in the body,
so long they ask after your welfare at home.
When the breath has gone and the body has perished,
your wife is afraid of that body. (6)
While a child, one is attached to play;
while a youth, one is attached to young women;
while old, one is attached to worry;
no one is attached to the supreme Brahman. (7)
Who is your beloved? Who is your son?
This worldly round is very strange.
Whose are you? Who are you? From where have you come?
Think on the truth of this, here, brother. (8)
From the company of the good, freedom from attachment;
from freedom from attachment, freedom from delusion;
from freedom from delusion, the unmoving truth;
from the unmoving truth, liberation while still living. (9)
When youth has gone, what stirring of desire?
When the water has dried up, what lake?
When wealth has dwindled, what family?
When the truth is known, what worldly round? (10)
Take no pride in wealth, in people, in youth:
time takes all of it away in the blink of an eye.
Leaving all this, which is made of illusion,
know the state of Brahman and enter it. (11)
Day and night, evening and morning,
winter and spring come back again.
Time plays, life goes by,
and still the wind of hope does not let go. (12)
In this cluster of twelve verses, in full,
this was told to the grammarian:
the teaching was given by the one skilled in learning,
the revered Lord Shankara. (12a)
What is this worry of yours about your beloved and your wealth?
Madman, have you no one to govern you?
In the three worlds the company of the good, and it alone,
becomes the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. (13)
One with matted locks, one shaven, one with his hair plucked out,
one who has put on many guises in ochre robes:
though he sees, the fool does not see;
for his belly's sake he has put on many guises. (14)
The limbs have grown weak, the head has turned grey,
the mouth has become toothless;
the old man goes about holding a stick,
and still he does not let go of the lump of hope. (15)
Fire in front, the sun behind;
at night, the knees drawn up to the chin;
alms in the palm of the hand, a dwelling at the foot of a tree:
and still the noose of hope does not let him go. (16)
One may make the journey to Gangasagar,
keep vows, or give gifts;
without knowledge, in the view of all,
one does not attain liberation even in a hundred births. (17)
Dwelling in temples of the gods or at the foot of trees,
the bare ground for a bed, a deer-skin for clothing,
giving up all possessions and enjoyment:
whom does such detachment not make happy? (18)
Whether delighting in yoga or delighting in pleasure,
whether delighting in company or without company,
he whose mind delights in Brahman
rejoices, rejoices, simply rejoices. (19)
One by whom the Bhagavad Gita has been studied even a little,
by whom a drop of the water of the Ganges has been drunk,
by whom the worship of Murari is performed even once:
with him Yama has no dispute. (20)
Birth again, death again,
lying again in a mother's womb:
here in this worldly round, so hard to cross,
shoreless, save me by your grace, O Murari. (21)
His patched cloak made of rags from the street,
his path free of merit and of sin,
the yogi, his mind fixed in yoga,
delights just like a child or a madman. (22)
Who are you? Who am I? From where has one come?
Who is my mother? Who is my father?
Consider all this to be without substance,
and leave the world, an imagining of dreams. (23)
In you, in me and elsewhere there is one Vishnu;
in vain you are angry with me, impatient.
Be even-minded everywhere,
if you wish soon for the state of Vishnu. (24)
With enemy, friend, son or kinsman
make no effort at quarrel or at peace.
See the Self in everything;
everywhere cast off the ignorance that sees difference. (25)
Leaving desire, anger, greed and delusion,
reflect on the Self: 'Who am I?'
Fools without knowledge of the Self
are cooked, hidden away in hell. (26)
The Gita and the Thousand Names are to be sung;
the form of the Lord of Shri is to be meditated on without end;
the mind is to be led into the company of the good;
and wealth is to be given to the poor. (27)
For pleasure one takes one's enjoyment of women;
afterwards, alas, disease in the body.
Though in the world death is the last refuge,
still one does not give up sinful conduct. (28)
Always consider wealth to be ruin:
truly, there is not a trace of happiness from it.
Those who have wealth fear even their own sons:
everywhere this is the established way. (29)
Control of the breath, withdrawal of the senses,
reflection that tells the lasting from the fleeting,
the practice of meditative absorption joined with recitation:
do these with care, with great care. (30)
Wholly devoted to the lotus feet of the guru,
be free soon of the worldly round.
Thus, by restraint of the senses and the mind,
you will see the god who dwells in your own heart. (31)
A certain foolish grammarian,
foremost in the study of 'ḍukṛñ karaṇe',
was taught by the disciples of the revered Lord Shankara
and had his faculties made pure. (32)
Worship Govinda, worship Govinda,
worship Govinda, O fool.
Other than the remembering of his name, any means
we do not see for crossing over worldly existence. (33)
rom: mā kuru dhana jana yauvana garvaṃ
kā me jananī ko me tātaḥ |
notes: Line references are stanza.line in the order of the text printed here: stanza 13 is the edition's verse 12a, so from stanza 14 on, stanza n is verse n-1. The verse numbers are kept at the ends of the verses, as (1) in the English and ||1|| in the romanization; the edition's १२अ is 12a.

The romanization follows the word divisions of the Devanagari as printed (so 'kāte', 'cana', 'vābhogaratovā', 'bhūtala majinaṃ', 'sajjanasaṃ gatirekā' are run together or split as there); ।, ॥ and the avagraha ऽ are written |, || and '.

Names: Govinda, Murari (Murāri, 'enemy of Mura') and Vishnu are names of the god Vishnu; Brahman is the absolute; Yama is the god of death; Shankara is the name given in the text itself (13.4, 33.3); the Lord of Shri (śrīpati, 28.2) is Vishnu as the husband of the goddess Śrī.
line 1.2 (and 34.2): bhajamūḍhamate, 'worship, O you of deluded mind'; mūḍhamati is the one addressed.
line 1.3: kāle, 'the time', here the time of death.
line 1.4 (and 33.2): ḍukṛñ karaṇe is a grammarian's entry in the list of verbal roots ('the root kṛ, in the sense of doing'); it stands for grammar rules learnt by rote. Kept in the original words.
line 3.3: māṃsāvasādi is read as māṃsa-vasā-ādi, 'flesh, fat and the like'.
line 5.2: stāvan carries over the -s of saktas in line 5.1 by sandhi (saktas tāvan).
line 5.4: vārtāṃ ... na pṛcchati, literally 'does not ask for news', i.e. no one asks how you are.
line 6.4: bibhyati, 'fears', is irregular for the expected bibheti.
saṃsāra (8.2, 10.4, 22.3, 32.2), the round of birth, death and rebirth and the worldly existence it entails, is rendered 'the worldly round'; bhava (14.4, 34.4) 'worldly existence'.
line 8.4: tattvaṃ cintaya tad iha bhrātaḥ can also be read 'think on that, the truth, here, brother'.
line 9.4: jīvanmukti, liberation attained while still alive.
line 10.1: vayasi gate, literally 'when age has gone', i.e. when the prime of life is past.
line 12.4 (and 16.4, 17.4): āśā is hope, longing or desire; here the longing that keeps one bound to the world.
line 13.1: mañjarikā, a cluster of blossoms; 'the twelve clusters' names the group of twelve verses ending here.
line 13.2: vaiyākaraṇasya, genitive, 'of the grammarian': told to him.
line 13.3: upadeśo bhūd stands for upadeśo 'bhūd ('the teaching was'), the avagraha not written.

line 13.4: bhagavaccharaṇaiḥ is an honorific plural, 'by the revered Lord'; it can be read as bhagavat + śaraṇaiḥ ('the Lord, the refuge') or as bhagavac-caraṇaiḥ ('the holy feet of the Lord'), both honorifics for the person.
line 14.1: kā te kāntā-dhana-gata-cintā, 'what is your worry concerning wife and wealth?'; kāntā may be 'wife' or 'beloved'.
line 15.3: cana is read ca na, 'and not'.
line 18.1: gaṅgāsāgara, Gangasagar, where the Ganges reaches the sea, a place of pilgrimage; it can also be read 'to the Ganges and to the sea'.
line 18.3: sarvamatena, 'by the opinion of all', i.e. as all schools agree.
line 19.2: ajina is the skin of an antelope or deer, worn by ascetics.
line 21.4: na carcā, 'no discussion, no questioning': Yama does not call him to account.
line 22.4: apāre, 'shoreless', belongs with saṃsāre in line 22.3.
line 24.1: āyātaḥ has no stated subject; 'one' is supplied.
line 24.4: svapna-vicāram, 'a dream-thought': the world seen as a figment of a dream.
line 26.2: vigraha-sandhi, quarrel and reconciliation (also war and peace).
line 27.2: ātmānaṃ bhāvaya ko 'ham can also be read 'reflect within yourself: who am I?'
line 28.1: gītā, the Bhagavad Gita; nāma sahasram, 'the thousand names', of Vishnu.
line 29.1: sukhataḥ can mean 'for pleasure' or 'readily'; rāmā is a woman.
line 29.3: maraṇaṃ śaraṇaṃ, 'death is the refuge', i.e. the only end or last resort.
line 30.1: artham anartham, a play on words: wealth (artha) is non-wealth, ruin (anartha).
lines 31.1-3: prāṇāyāma (control of the breath), pratyāhāra (withdrawal of the senses) and samādhi (meditative absorption) are terms of yoga; jāpya is the repeated recitation of prayers or names.
line 33.4: śodhitakaraṇaḥ, 'whose karaṇas (faculties, instruments of knowing) were purified'; karaṇa also echoes 'ḍukṛñ karaṇe' in 33.2.
